mainTopic: The five payments of a חובל, and the proofs that "עין תחת עין" means money
overview: This amud opens the eighth פרק of בבא קמא with a new משנה about a חובל, someone who injures another person. He owes five payments: נזק, צער, ריפוי, שבת and בושת. The משנה explains how each one is measured, such as valuing the victim as an עבד in the market for נזק and as a cucumber guard for שבת. The גמרא then asks why he pays money at all, when the תורה says "עין תחת עין". A ברייתא gives two proofs: comparing one who strikes a person to one who strikes an animal, and the פסוק forbidding כופר only for a murderer. The גמרא tests both proofs, defends them, and shows that each one teaches something different. Next, רבי דוסתאי בן יהודה argues that a big eye and a small eye cannot be an equal exchange, so the תורה must mean money. The חכמים push back that the תורה may mean taking away sight, and their argument continues on the next amud.

steps.title: One who injures another owes five payments
steps.stepSummary: The משנה states the main rule: a חובל must pay for נזק, צער, ריפוי, שבת and בושת.
steps.simpleTranslation: One who injures another person must pay him for five things: damage, pain, medical costs, lost work time, and embarrassment.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה opens the chapter with its main rule. Whoever injures another person owes him five separate kinds of payment.
steps.deeperAnalysis: These are five different losses, not one. A single injury can make all five payments due at once. The rest of the משנה goes through them one at a time.

keyTerms.meaning: Damage: the permanent loss in the victim's value
Loss of work time while the victim is laid up

steps.whyThisMatters: This list of five payments is the framework for the whole perek. Every later discussion goes back to one of these five.

phrases.english: MISHNA: One who injures his fellow
is liable to him for five things:
for damage, for pain, for medical costs,
for loss of work, and for humiliation.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַתְנִי׳ הַחוֹבֵל בַּחֲבֵירוֹ חַיָּיב עָלָיו מִשּׁוּם חֲמִשָּׁה דְּבָרִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new chapter and a new משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A חובל owes five separate payments: נזק, צער, ריפוי, שבת and בושת.

steps.title: How damage is measured: the slave-market comparison
steps.stepSummary: נזק is measured by valuing the victim as an עבד in the market before and after the injury and paying the difference.
steps.simpleTranslation: How is damage paid? If he blinded his eye, cut off his hand, or broke his leg, we picture the victim as a slave being sold in the market. We estimate how much he was worth before and how much he is worth now.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה now explains the first payment, נזק. It gives a way to put a price on a lost limb.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A free person has no market price, so the משנה borrows the price of an עבד. The court figures out what such a person would have sold for before the injury and what he would sell for now. The difference is the נזק payment.

keyTerms.meaning: How? (the משנה is about to explain)
A slave sold in the market

steps.confusionAlert: The victim is not actually a slave, and nobody sells him. The עבד comparison is only a measuring tool to turn a lost limb into a money amount.

phrases.english: For damage, how?

phrases.aramaic: סִימֵּא אֶת עֵינוֹ; קָטַע אֶת יָדוֹ;
phrases.english: If he blinded his eye, cut off his hand,
or broke his leg –
we view him as though he were
a slave being sold in the market,
and we assess how much he was worth
and how much he is worth now.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the first of the five payments listed in step 1.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: נזק equals the drop in the victim's value as if he were an עבד sold in the market.

steps.title: How pain is measured, even with no lasting wound
steps.stepSummary: צער is paid even for a burn on the fingernail that leaves no wound. The amount is what a similar person would accept to go through that pain.
steps.simpleTranslation: Pain: if he burned him with a skewer or a nail, even on his fingernail where it leaves no wound, we estimate how much a person like this would want to be paid to suffer this way.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה explains the second payment, צער. It shows that pain is paid for on its own, even when there is no damage at all.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The fingernail case matters because nothing there loses value, so there is no נזק. The משנה still makes him pay for the pain alone. The amount is measured by how much someone like the victim would accept to endure this suffering.

phrases.english: Pain: if he burned him with a skewer
phrases.notes: Some versions leave out the word in round brackets, so it reads simply 'he burned him with a skewer.'

phrases.english: or with a nail,
and even on his fingernail,
a place where it does not make a wound –
we estimate how much a person like this one
would want to take to suffer this way.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the second of the five payments.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: צער is paid even with no physical damage. It is measured by what a comparable person would accept to endure that pain.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that each of the five payments stands on its own. צער is owed even when there is no נזק.

steps.title: Medical costs: what the injurer must cover
steps.stepSummary: The injurer must pay to heal the victim. This covers growths caused by the blow and a wound that keeps reopening, but not anything after the wound has fully healed.
steps.simpleTranslation: Medical costs: if he hit him, he must pay to heal him. If growths came up, he pays if they came from the blow, and not if they did not. If the wound healed and reopened, again and again, he must keep paying. If it healed completely, he no longer has to pay.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה explains the third payment, ריפוי. It also sets the limits of what the injurer has to cover.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The test is whether the problem comes from the blow. Growths caused by the blow, or a wound that keeps reopening, are his responsibility. Unrelated growths, or anything after a full recovery, are not.

keyTerms.meaning: Growths, such as blisters or sores

steps.whatToRemember: The five payments are נזק, צער, ריפוי, שבת and בושת. נזק uses the slave-market comparison. צער uses what a similar person would accept for the pain. ריפוי covers healing for anything caused by the blow, until the wound has fully healed.

phrases.english: Medical costs: if he struck him, he is liable to heal him.
If growths came up on him,
if they are because of the blow, he is liable;
if not because of the blow, he is exempt.
If it healed and reopened, healed and reopened –
he is liable to heal him.
If it healed completely –
he is not liable to heal him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the third of the five payments.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The injurer pays medical costs for anything caused by the blow, including repeated reopening, but not for unrelated growths or after a full recovery.

steps.title: How payment for lost work time is measured
steps.stepSummary: שבת is paid as if the victim were a cucumber guard, since his limb was already paid for.
steps.simpleTranslation: Loss of work: we view the injured person as if he were a cucumber guard, because the injurer already paid him for his hand and his leg.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה explains how to calculate שבת, the money for work the victim misses while he heals.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The victim is paid only the wage of a very easy job, like guarding cucumbers. He already got paid under נזק for losing the limb, and that payment covered what the limb was worth to his career. So שבת pays for the work time he loses while healing, at the wage of a light job he could still do after the injury.

keyTerms.meaning: Payment for lost work time while the victim is healing
A cucumber guard, a very easy and low-paid job
The value of his hand, already paid under נזק

steps.confusionAlert: שבת is not the victim's full normal salary. His bigger, long-term loss was already paid under נזק, so here he only gets the wage of a light job.

phrases.english: Loss of work: we view him
as if he were a guard of cucumbers,
phrases.notes: A cucumber guard just sits and watches, so it is a job even an injured person can still do.

phrases.english: since he already gave him
the value of his hand and the value of his leg.
phrases.notes: This is the נזק payment from step 2.

steps.triggerLanguage: שֶׁבֶת – רוֹאִין אוֹתוֹ כְּאִילּוּ הוּא שׁוֹמֵר קִישּׁוּאִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the משנה's list, moving from ריפוי to שבת.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: שבת is paid at the wage of a cucumber guard, since the limb's full value was already paid under נזק.

steps.title: How payment for embarrassment is measured
steps.stepSummary: בושת depends on the status of the one who embarrasses and the one who is embarrassed.
steps.simpleTranslation: Embarrassment: it all depends on who did the embarrassing and who was embarrassed.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה gives the last of the five payments, בושת, and says there is no single fixed amount.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The amount changes with the people involved. Being embarrassed by a certain person, or being a certain kind of person, makes the shame bigger or smaller, so בית דין looks at both sides.

keyTerms.meaning: Payment for embarrassment caused by the injury
The one who causes the embarrassment

steps.whatToRemember: All five payments of the חובל: נזק (market value as an עבד), צער (what a person would accept to suffer the pain), ריפוי (medical costs), שבת (cucumber guard wage), בושת (depends on both people).

phrases.english: Embarrassment: it all depends on
the one who embarrasses and the one who is embarrassed.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the משנה's list of five payments.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The amount of בושת depends on the status of both the one who embarrasses and the one embarrassed.

steps.title: Doesn't the Torah say an actual eye for an eye?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the משנה assumes the injurer pays money, when the תורה says "עין תחת עין".
steps.simpleTranslation: Why should he pay money? The תורה says "an eye for an eye." Maybe it means a real eye!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins and challenges the whole basis of the משנה: why money at all?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה took for granted that a חובל pays money. But the plain words "עין תחת עין" sound like the injurer should lose his own eye. The גמרא wants a source showing the תורה means money.

keyTerms.meaning: The Merciful One, meaning the תורה or ה׳

phrases.english: Gemara: Why?
phrases.notes: Why does the משנה just assume he pays money?

phrases.english: The Merciful One said "an eye for an eye";
phrases.notes: שמות 21:24

phrases.english: say it means an actual eye!

steps.triggerLanguage: אַמַּאי? ״עַיִן תַּחַת עַיִן״ אָמַר רַחֲמָנָא – אֵימָא עַיִן מַמָּשׁ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns from the משנה to the גמרא, challenging the משנה's basic assumption of money payment.
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's assumption that a חובל pays money for נזק.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The plain meaning of "עין תחת עין" points to a physical punishment, taking the injurer's own eye, not a money payment.

steps.title: A ברייתא proves the injurer pays money
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא compares hitting a person to hitting an animal: both mean paying money.
steps.simpleTranslation: Don't think that. A ברייתא teaches: You might think that if he blinded someone's eye, we blind his eye; if he cut off a hand, we cut off his hand; if he broke a leg, we break his leg. That is why the verse says "one who strikes a person" and "one who strikes an animal." Just as one who strikes an animal pays money, so one who strikes a person pays money.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the literal reading and brings a ברייתא proving that the injurer pays money.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא first raises the same idea as the question, that we would injure the injurer in return. Then it uses two phrases the תורה places side by side, "מכה אדם" and "מכה בהמה". Everyone agrees hurting an animal means paying money, so hurting a person must also mean paying money.

keyTerms.meaning: As was taught in a ברייתא

steps.confusionAlert: "עין תחת עין" does not mean we really take out the injurer's eye. The הלכה reads it as paying the value of an eye.
steps.whatToRemember: A חובל pays money, not his own eye. The source is the comparison between "מכה אדם" and "מכה בהמה": just as one who hurts an animal pays, so does one who hurts a person.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is the foundation for the whole פרק. Every payment in the משנה only makes sense once we know "עין תחת עין" means money.

phrases.english: That should not enter your mind;
as it was taught: One might think, if he blinded his eye,
we blind his eye,

phrases.aramaic: קָטַע אֶת יָדוֹ – מְקַטֵּעַ אֶת יָדוֹ,
phrases.english: if he cut off his hand, we cut off his hand,

phrases.aramaic: שִׁיבֵּר אֶת רַגְלוֹ – מְשַׁבֵּר אֶת רַגְלוֹ?
phrases.english: if he broke his leg, we break his leg?
The verse teaches: "one who strikes a person" and "one who strikes an animal";
phrases.notes: ויקרא 24:17–21, where the two appear close together.

phrases.english: just as one who strikes an animal is liable to pay money,
so too one who strikes a person is liable to pay money.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 7 by bringing a ברייתא.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Brings a source (ברייתא) showing the verse means money.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: "עין תחת עין" means physically taking the injurer's eye, hand, or leg.
steps.terutzMaskana: Comparing "מכה אדם" to "מכה בהמה" shows that injuring a person means paying money, just like injuring an animal.
steps.raayaObject: That a חובל pays money and is not injured in return.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא comparing "מכה אדם" to "מכה בהמה".

steps.title: A backup proof from the ban on taking ransom for a murderer
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא brings a second proof: כופר is forbidden only for a murderer, so it is allowed for cutting off limbs that do not grow back.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you want to push back on that proof, look at the פסוק: "Do not take ransom for the life of a murderer." Only for a murderer do you not take ransom. But you do take ransom for main limbs that don't grow back.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא offers a second proof that the injurer pays money, in case someone objects to the comparison with an animal.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The תורה says not to take כופר for a murderer's life. By saying 'for a murderer,' it implies that for a lesser loss, such as a limb that will never grow back, money is taken. A lost limb is like a small 'death' of that limb, yet money is accepted for it.

keyTerms.meaning: If you wish to object, here is another proof
Ransom money paid in place of a punishment
Main limbs, such as a hand, foot, or eye

phrases.english: And if you wish to say [otherwise],
the verse says:
"You shall not take ransom for the life of a murderer,
phrases.notes: במדבר 35:31

phrases.english: who is guilty of death"

phrases.aramaic: לְנֶפֶשׁ רוֹצֵחַ אִי אַתָּה לוֹקֵחַ כּוֹפֶר,
phrases.english: for the life of a murderer you do not take ransom,
but you do take ransom
for main limbs, which do not grow back.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִם נַפְשְׁךָ לוֹמַר, הֲרֵי הוּא אוֹמֵר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a second source for the same conclusion reached in step 8.
steps.raayaObject: That cutting off a limb is paid for with money and not with the injurer's own limb.
steps.raayaSupportSource: במדבר 35:31, read as limiting the ban on כופר to a murderer only.
steps.whyThisMatters: This proof does not depend on comparing a person to an animal, so it stands even if that comparison is weakened.

steps.title: Which verse about striking does the ברייתא mean?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks which פסוק the ברייתא's comparison of hitting a person and hitting an animal comes from.
steps.simpleTranslation: Which "one who strikes" is the ברייתא talking about?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to the ברייתא from step 8 and asks exactly which פסוק it is quoting. This sets up the next few steps.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא spoke of 'one who strikes an animal' and 'one who strikes a person' as if from a פסוק. The גמרא wants to find that פסוק, because the comparison only works if it fits.

phrases.english: Which "one who strikes"?
phrases.notes: He means: which פסוק was the ברייתא from step 8 quoting?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns from the backup proof to examine the first proof in step 8.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The exact פסוק behind the ברייתא's comparison of hitting an animal and hitting a person.

steps.title: Not the verse about killing
steps.stepSummary: The first suggested פסוק does not work, because it is about killing a person, not injuring him.
steps.simpleTranslation: If you say it is "One who strikes an animal shall pay for it, and one who strikes a person shall be put to death," that פסוק is talking about killing!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא suggests one פסוק and immediately rejects it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: That פסוק says the one who strikes a person 'shall be put to death,' so it is about murder. There is no money payment for murder, so this פסוק cannot teach that injuries are paid with money.

keyTerms.meaning: If you say (a suggestion about to be rejected)

phrases.english: If you say: "One who strikes an animal shall pay for it,
phrases.notes: ויקרא 24:21

phrases.english: and one who strikes a person shall be put to death"
that is written about killing!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tests a first answer to the question of step 10 and rejects it.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects ויקרא 24:21 as the source of the ברייתא's comparison.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: That פסוק is about killing, where no money is paid, so it cannot teach a money payment for injury.

steps.title: The verses about killing an animal and maiming a person, side by side
steps.stepSummary: The source is the פסוק about killing an animal, which says pay, together with the פסוק right after it about maiming a person.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, it is from here: "One who kills an animal shall pay for it, a life for a life." And right next to it: "If a man maims his fellow, as he did, so shall be done to him."
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives its real answer: two פסוקים sitting next to each other, one about an animal and one about injuring a person.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For the animal, the תורה clearly means paying money. The very next פסוק talks about injuring a person, and because the two sit together, we learn that the person's injury is also paid with money.

phrases.english: Rather, from here:
"One who kills an animal shall pay for it,
phrases.notes: ויקרא 24:18

phrases.english: a life for a life",
and right next to it:
"And if a man maims his fellow,
phrases.notes: ויקרא 24:19

phrases.english: as he has done, so shall be done to him."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces the rejected פסוק of step 11 with the correct source.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: ויקרא 24:18 (killing an animal, which is paid with money) placed next to ויקרא 24:19 (maiming a person).

steps.title: But the verse about a person does not say "strikes"
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects that the פסוק about maiming a person does not use the word 'strikes' at all.
steps.simpleTranslation: But this one does not say "one who strikes"!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the answer it just gave.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא compared 'one who strikes an animal' to 'one who strikes a person.' The פסוק about the person says 'maims,' not 'strikes,' so the word the comparison seems to depend on is missing.

phrases.english: This is not "one who strikes"!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the source proposed in step 12.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that ויקרא 24:19 is the 'one who strikes a person' that the ברייתא meant.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא's wording does not match the פסוק's wording, so the פסוק seems to be the wrong source.

steps.title: The comparison is about the act of striking, not the exact word
steps.stepSummary: The comparison is based on the act of hitting in both cases. Since hitting an animal means paying, hitting a person also means paying.
steps.simpleTranslation: We are comparing hitting to hitting. Just as hitting written about an animal leads to payment, so too hitting written about a person leads to payment.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the ברייתא was describing the act of hitting, not quoting the exact word of the פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Maiming a person is also a kind of hitting, even if the פסוק does not use that word. So the rule matches: an animal's injury is paid with money, and a person's injury is paid with money too.

phrases.english: We are saying "striking" and "striking":
just as striking stated about an animal leads to payment,
so too striking stated about a person leads to payment.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 13.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefines the comparison as based on the act, not on the exact wording.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא's comparison needs the same word, 'strikes,' in both פסוקים.
steps.terutzMaskana: The comparison rests on the act of hitting, which both cases share, so a person's injury is paid with money like an animal's.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not look for the word מכה in the פסוק about the person. The גמרא admits it is not there; the comparison is about what happened, not the word used.

steps.title: But the verse says "he shall surely be put to death"
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges with a פסוק in the same section that says the one who strikes a person 'shall be put to death.'
steps.simpleTranslation: But it is written: "And a man who strikes any person shall surely be put to death"!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא raises a new challenge against the conclusion that injuries are paid with money.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This פסוק, in the same section about injuries, sounds like a real physical punishment. That would suggest the injurer loses something of his own body, not just money.

keyTerms.meaning: He shall surely be put to death

phrases.english: But isn't it written:
"And a man who strikes any person
phrases.notes: ויקרא 24:17

phrases.english: shall surely be put to death"!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהָא כְּתִיב וְאִישׁ כִּי יַכֶּה כׇּל נֶפֶשׁ אָדָם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the conclusion of step 14 using a nearby פסוק.
steps.kashyaTarget: The conclusion that hitting a person leads only to payment.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The nearby פסוק uses language of physical punishment, which suggests the injurer is punished in his body.

steps.title: It means with money
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that 'shall be put to death' here means paying money.
steps.simpleTranslation: With money.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a very short answer: the פסוק is about money.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even though the words sound like real death, the גמרא reads them as a money payment. That keeps this פסוק in line with the comparison to an animal in step 14.

phrases.english: With money.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 15.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reinterprets the פסוק as a money payment.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'Shall be put to death' means a real physical punishment.
steps.terutzMaskana: The פסוק is talking about paying money.

steps.title: How do we know it means money and not real death?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for proof that the פסוק means money, since its plain meaning is real death.
steps.simpleTranslation: How do you know it means money? Say it means actual death!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on its own short answer and asks for a source. The next step answers this.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Saying 'with money' is not enough when the words plainly say death. The גמרא wants a reason to leave the simple meaning, which sets up the next part of the discussion.

phrases.english: From where do you know that it is with money?
Say it means actual death!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer of step 16 by asking for its source.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The plain words say death, so reading them as money needs proof.

steps.title: Two reasons the death penalty reading is impossible
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא proves that 'מות יומת' cannot mean real death. First, it is placed next to 'מכה בהמה ישלמנה'. Second, a later פסוק uses the word 'given', which points to money.
steps.simpleTranslation: That idea should not enter your mind. Reason one: this פסוק is linked to 'One who strikes an animal shall pay for it.' Reason two: right after it the פסוק says 'As he gave a blemish to a person, so shall it be given to him,' and 'given' shows it means money.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question from step 17. It gives two reasons why the פסוק must mean money and not real death.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Reason one: the פסוק about hitting a person sits right next to the פסוק about hitting an animal, where the punishment is clearly payment. So the two should match. Reason two: the word 'יִנָּתֵן' (shall be given) is language of handing something over, and that fits money.

keyTerms.meaning: It should not enter your mind; that idea is impossible
It was linked or compared, because the two פסוקים sit side by side
Shall be given; shows that something is handed over, which means money

phrases.english: That should not enter your mind.
One reason: because it is juxtaposed
to 'One who strikes an animal shall pay for it.'
phrases.notes: ויקרא 24:18

phrases.english: And furthermore, it is written after it:
'As he has given a blemish to a person,'
phrases.notes: ויקרא 24:20

phrases.english: 'so shall it be given to him'
and learn from it that it means money.
phrases.notes: The point is the word 'given': you give money, so this is talking about payment.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the demand for proof in step 17
steps.terutzResolutionType: Two separate textual proofs: placement next to another פסוק, and the wording of a later פסוק
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'מות יומת' might mean real death for maiming a person
steps.terutzMaskana: The פסוק means money: it is linked to 'מכה בהמה ישלמנה', and 'יִנָּתֶן' is money language

steps.title: What did the ברייתא mean by 'if you want to say'?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the ברייתא opened its second proof with 'אם נפשך לומר', which hints that the first proof had a problem.
steps.simpleTranslation: And what is meant by 'If it is your wish to say'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא turns back to the wording of the ברייתא. It asks what weakness in the first proof made the ברייתא add a second one. This sets up the next steps.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The phrase 'אם נפשך לומר' usually means: 'if you want to argue against the first proof, here is another one.' So the גמרא wants to know what the argument against the first proof was.

keyTerms.meaning: If it is your wish to say; introduces a backup proof because the first one can be questioned

phrases.english: And what is meant by 'If it is your wish to say'?
phrases.notes: This phrase comes from the ברייתא quoted earlier on the daf, right before its second proof.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the first proof is finished, the גמרא asks about the ברייתא's move to a second proof
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What weakness in the first proof led the ברייתא to add 'אם נפשך לומר'

steps.title: Why learn from hitting an animal and not from hitting a person?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains that the תנא saw a weakness: perhaps we should learn from 'מכה אדם' (death) instead of 'מכה בהמה' (payment).
steps.simpleTranslation: There was a further difficulty troubling the תנא: what made you learn from 'one who strikes an animal'? Learn instead from 'one who strikes a person'!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers its question by showing what bothered the תנא. The first proof chose to compare to hitting an animal, but one could compare to killing a person instead.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both 'מכה בהמה' and 'מכה אדם' use the word 'hitting', so either could be the model. If we compare to 'מכה אדם', which is real death, then maiming would get a bodily punishment and not money. That is the weak spot in the first proof.

keyTerms.meaning: What did you see? Why choose this side over the other?
One who strikes (kills) a person; punished by death

phrases.english: A further difficulty was troubling the tanna:
What did you see that you derive
from 'one who strikes an animal'?
Let him derive from 'one who strikes a person'!
phrases.notes: ויקרא 24:21, where the one who kills a person is put to death.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 19 by stating the challenge that bothered the תנא
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The תנא worried that one could just as well compare to 'מכה אדם' (death) instead of 'מכה בהמה' (payment)
steps.kashyaTarget: The comparison to 'מכה בהמה' from step 14
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The 'hitting' link works just as well with 'מכה אדם', which leads to a bodily punishment

steps.title: Learn damages from damages, not from death
steps.stepSummary: The answer: cases of injury should be learned from other injury cases, not from a case of killing.
steps.simpleTranslation: They say: we learn damages from damages, and we do not learn damages from death.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends the first proof. Maiming is an injury, and hitting an animal is also an injury case, so they are the better match.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Killing a person is a totally different kind of case: a death penalty, not damage to something. Maiming is like hurting an animal, since both are damage that leaves the victim alive. So the better comparison is to the animal case, which means paying money.

keyTerms.meaning: We judge or learn one case from another

phrases.english: They say:
We derive damages from damages,
and we do not derive damages from death.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Defends the first proof against the challenge in step 20
steps.terutzResolutionType: Choosing the closer comparison by type of case
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Maiming might be learned from 'מכה אדם' and get a death-like punishment
steps.terutzMaskana: Injury is learned from injury ('מכה בהמה'), not from killing, so it means payment

steps.title: On the contrary: learn a person from a person
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא pushes back: maybe the better rule is that a case about a person should be learned from a case about a person, not from an animal.
steps.simpleTranslation: On the contrary! We learn a person from a person, and we do not learn a person from an animal!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the answer in step 21. It offers an equally good reason to pick the other side.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 21 matched by type of case (injury with injury). Now the גמרא says we could just as well match by who was hurt (a person with a person). That would point back to 'מכה אדם' and a bodily punishment, so the first proof is still unclear.

keyTerms.meaning: On the contrary; the opposite argument is just as strong

steps.confusionAlert: Do not think the גמרא has now decided that maiming means bodily punishment. It is only showing that both comparisons are equally strong. That is why a separate proof is needed in the next step.

phrases.english: On the contrary!
We derive a person from a person,
and we do not derive a person from an animal!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer of step 21 with an opposite, equally strong rule
steps.kashyaTarget: The rule 'דנין נזיקין מנזיקין' in step 21
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Matching by the victim (a person) is just as reasonable as matching by the type of case, and it points to 'מכה אדם'

steps.title: The second proof: no ransom only for a murderer
steps.stepSummary: Because the first proof can be argued either way, the ברייתא brings the פסוק 'לא תקחו כפר לנפש רצח'. Money is forbidden only for a murderer, so money is taken for limbs that cannot grow back.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is why the ברייתא says 'If it is your wish to say': the פסוק says 'Do not take ransom for the life of a murderer, who is guilty of death, for he shall surely die.' For the life of a murderer you may not take ransom, but you may take ransom for main limbs that do not grow back.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes answering step 19. Since the first proof stays unclear, the ברייתא brings a separate proof from the פסוק about כופר.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק forbids taking money only in the case of a murderer. That implies that for cutting off a limb, which is like the 'death' of a part of the body, money is accepted. This proof stands on its own and does not need the animal-or-person comparison at all.

keyTerms.meaning: This is what is taught; this explains the wording
Ransom; money paid in place of a bodily punishment

steps.whatToRemember: 'עין תחת עין' means money. The first proof compares to 'מכה בהמה', but that comparison can be argued either way. So the ברייתא adds a second proof: the פסוק forbids כופר only for a murderer, which means כופר is taken for limbs that are lost.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is a central source for the הלכה that a person who injures another pays money and is not physically maimed in return.

phrases.english: This is why it teaches 'If it is your wish to say':
Behold, it says:
'Do not take ransom for the life of a murderer'
phrases.notes: במדבר 35:31

phrases.english: 'who is guilty of death,'
'for he shall surely die.'

phrases.aramaic: לְנֶפֶשׁ רוֹצֵחַ אִי אַתָּה לוֹקֵחַ כּוֹפֶר,
phrases.english: For the life of a murderer you do not take ransom,
but you do take ransom
for main limbs that do not grow back.
phrases.notes: Losing a limb is like a 'death' of that part of the body, yet here money is allowed.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the deadlock of steps 21 and 22 by pointing to the ברייתא's independent second proof, which completes the answer to step 19
steps.terutzResolutionType: Replacing a disputed comparison with an independent proof from another פסוק
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Since the comparison could go either way, maiming might get a bodily punishment
steps.terutzMaskana: The כופר פסוק shows money is accepted for lost limbs, only not for a murderer
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Injuring a person's limbs is paid with money, proven from 'לא תקחו כפר לנפש רצח'

steps.title: The verse is needed for a different lesson
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the proof from 'לא תקחו כפר'. That פסוק seems to be needed to teach that a murderer cannot get two punishments: paying money and also being killed.
steps.simpleTranslation: Is this verse, 'You shall not take ransom for the life of a murderer,' really coming to exclude cut-off limbs? It is needed to teach: don't do two things to him. Don't take money from him and also kill him!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the proof from step 23. It says the פסוק is already used for a different lesson, so it cannot also teach about limbs.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 23 read 'לנפש רצח' to mean that only a murderer cannot pay money, so an injurer does pay. Now the גמרא suggests the פסוק has a different job: forbidding a double punishment of money plus death. If that is its job, the proof about limbs falls away.

keyTerms.meaning: Limbs and body parts (like a hand or an eye) that do not grow back once cut off
It is needed for (a different lesson)
'The Merciful One', meaning the Torah or ה׳
Don't do two things to him, meaning don't punish him twice

phrases.english: And this verse, 'You shall not take ransom for the life of a murderer' —
is it really coming to exclude limbs that don't grow back?
This verse is needed

phrases.aramaic: דְּאָמַר רַחֲמָנָא לָא תַּעֲבֵיד בֵּיהּ תַּרְתֵּי –
phrases.english: to teach what the Merciful One says: don't do two things to him —
don't take money from him and also kill him!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the proof that ended step 23
steps.kashyaTarget: The reading of 'לא תקחו כפר לנפש רצח' as excluding ראשי אברים
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A פסוק already used for one lesson (no double punishment) cannot be used for a second lesson

steps.title: The no-double-punishment rule comes from another verse
steps.stepSummary: The rule against two punishments is learned from 'כדי רשעתו' ('according to his wickedness'), so 'לא תקחו כפר' is free to teach about limbs.
steps.simpleTranslation: That lesson comes from 'according to his wickedness': for one wickedness you can make him liable, but you cannot make him liable for two wickednesses.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge. The ban on double punishment has its own source, so our פסוק is still free.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'רשעתו' is written in the singular, which shows that one sin brings only one punishment. Since that lesson comes from a different פסוק, 'לא תקחו כפר' does not need to teach it.

keyTerms.meaning: 'According to his wickedness' (singular), the פסוק about מלקות
It comes out of, meaning it is learned from
One wickedness, meaning one punishment for one act

phrases.english: That is learned from 'according to his wickedness' —
phrases.notes: דברים 25:2. The word 'wickedness' is singular, and that is the key.

phrases.english: for one wickedness you can make him liable,
but you cannot make him liable for two wickednesses.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 24
steps.terutzResolutionType: Alternate source for the competing lesson
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'לא תקחו כפר' is needed to forbid money plus death
steps.terutzMaskana: That rule comes from 'כדי רשעתו', so 'לא תקחו כפר' is free

steps.title: The verse is needed for its plain meaning
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא pushes again: the פסוק is still needed for its simple meaning, that you cannot take money and let a murderer go free.
steps.simpleTranslation: But it is still needed for what the Merciful One says: don't take money and let him go free!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a second challenge. Even without the double-punishment idea, the פסוק has its own plain lesson: a murderer cannot buy his way out of death.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This attack is stronger, because it uses the plain meaning of the פסוק itself. If the whole פסוק is needed just to forbid ransom instead of death, nothing is left over to teach about limbs.

keyTerms.meaning: And still, meaning there is still a problem
And let him go free (from the death penalty)

phrases.english: But it is still needed
for what the Merciful One says:
don't take money and let him go free!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new challenge after step 25 answered the first one
steps.kashyaTarget: Using 'לא תקחו כפר' to exclude ראשי אברים
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The plain meaning of the פסוק (no ransom instead of death) uses it up

steps.title: The extra words 'for the life of a murderer'
steps.stepSummary: The plain lesson only needed 'לא תקחו כפר לאשר הוא רשע למות'. The extra words 'לנפש רצח' teach that only a murderer cannot pay, but limbs that don't grow back are paid with money.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, the Torah could have written 'You shall not take ransom for one who is guilty of death.' Why do I need 'for the life of a murderer'? Learn from this: for a murderer you don't take ransom, but you do take ransom for limbs that don't grow back.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers by pointing to extra words in the פסוק. The plain lesson is covered by part of the פסוק, so the extra words teach about limbs.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words 'לאשר הוא רשע למות' alone would have taught that a murderer cannot buy his life. Adding 'לנפש רצח' narrows the ban to taking a life. So for injuries, money is exactly what is taken. This repeats the conclusion of step 23, but now it rests on firmer ground.

keyTerms.meaning: Why do I need it? (points to extra words)

steps.whatToRemember: The extra words 'לנפש רצח' show that only for a life is money refused. For limbs that cannot grow back, the injurer pays money.

phrases.english: If so, let the Merciful One write

phrases.aramaic: ״לֹא תִקְּחוּ כוֹפֶר לַאֲשֶׁר הוּא רָשָׁע לָמוּת״;
phrases.english: 'You shall not take ransom for one who is guilty of death';
phrases.notes: This is the same פסוק with only the words 'for the life of a murderer' taken out.

phrases.english: why do I need 'for the life of a murderer'?
Learn from this:

phrases.aramaic: לְנֶפֶשׁ רוֹצֵחַ אִי אַתָּה לוֹקֵחַ כּוֹפֶר,
phrases.english: for the life of a murderer you do not take ransom,
but you do take ransom
for limbs that do not grow back.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 26
steps.terutzResolutionType: Extra words in the פסוק (יתור לשון)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The whole פסוק is needed for 'no ransom instead of death'
steps.terutzMaskana: 'לנפש רצח' is extra and teaches that money is taken for ראשי אברים

steps.title: Why is the first proof still needed?
steps.stepSummary: If 'לא תקחו כפר' already proves that injuries are paid with money, why does the ברייתא also need the 'מכה–מכה' comparison?
steps.simpleTranslation: And since it is written 'You shall not take ransom,' why do I need the 'strikes'–'strikes' comparison?
steps.whatsHappening: Now that the second proof stands, the גמרא asks why the first proof is needed at all.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The Torah does not teach the same thing twice. If the פסוק of כופר is enough, the comparison between striking a person and striking an animal looks extra. The גמרא wants to know what it adds.

keyTerms.meaning: The comparison between 'one who strikes' a person and 'one who strikes' an animal

phrases.english: And since it is written 'You shall not take ransom,'
why do I need the 'strikes'–'strikes' comparison?
phrases.notes: This is the ברייתא's first proof: one who strikes an animal pays, so one who strikes a person pays too.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: With the second proof secured, turns back to ask why the first proof is needed
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If one source already teaches the law, a second source looks extra

steps.title: Without the comparison, the injurer could choose
steps.stepSummary: From 'לא תקחו כפר' alone we might think the injurer may choose between giving his own eye and paying its value. The animal comparison teaches that he must pay money.
steps.simpleTranslation: They say: if we had only this verse, I would have thought that if he wants, he gives his eye, and if he wants, he gives the value of his eye. So it teaches us from an animal: just as one who strikes an animal pays money, so too one who strikes a person pays money.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא shows that each proof teaches something different. The animal comparison removes the option of giving up one's own eye.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'לא תקחו כפר' only shows that money is allowed for injuries. It does not show that money is required. The comparison to striking an animal, where only money is ever paid, teaches that payment is the only option.

keyTerms.meaning: They say (the answer given in the בית המדרש)
The money value of his eye

steps.whatToRemember: Two proofs, two jobs: 'לא תקחו כפר' shows money is allowed for injuries, and 'מכה–מכה' shows money is the only way to pay.

phrases.english: They say: if we had only this verse,
I would have thought:
if he wants, he gives his own eye,
and if he wants, he gives the value of his eye;
so it teaches us from an animal:
just as one who strikes an animal must pay money,
so too one who strikes a person must pay money.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 28
steps.terutzResolutionType: Each source teaches a different point
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The injurer could choose between giving his eye and paying
steps.terutzMaskana: The animal comparison makes money the only option

steps.title: רבי דוסתאי says 'eye for an eye' means money
steps.stepSummary: A new ברייתא: רבי דוסתאי בן יהודה says 'עין תחת עין' means money, and he asks whether it might mean a real eye.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was taught: רבי דוסתאי בן יהודה says, 'An eye for an eye' means money. You say money, but maybe it means an actual eye?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new proof. רבי דוסתאי states his position and raises the opposite possibility, setting up his argument in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This starts a new series of proofs that injuries are paid with money. The question 'or maybe an actual eye?' is not a real doubt. It sets up the proof that follows.

keyTerms.meaning: It was taught in a ברייתא

phrases.aramaic: תַּנְיָא, רַבִּי דּוֹסְתַּאי בֶּן יְהוּדָה אוֹמֵר:
phrases.english: It was taught: Rabbi Dostai ben Yehuda says:
'An eye for an eye' means money.
phrases.notes: ויקרא 24:20

phrases.english: You say money,
or does it mean only an actual eye?

steps.triggerLanguage: תַּנְיָא, רַבִּי דּוֹסְתַּאי בֶּן יְהוּדָה אוֹמֵר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins a new ברייתא with another proof for the same law

steps.title: A big eye and a small eye are not equal
steps.stepSummary: If one person's eye is big and the other's is small, taking a real eye would not be 'an eye for an eye'. So the פסוק must mean money.
steps.simpleTranslation: You can answer: suppose one man's eye was big and the other man's eye was small. How can I call this 'an eye for an eye'?
steps.whatsHappening: רבי דוסתאי gives his proof. Taking an actual eye cannot always be an exact match.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'תחת' means an equal exchange. When the eyes differ in size, taking a real eye would not be equal, so the פסוק cannot mean that. A fair money value can always be equal.

keyTerms.meaning: How can I apply this phrase to it?
In place of, an equal exchange

phrases.english: You can answer: here is a case where
the eye of this one was big
and the eye of that one was small,

phrases.aramaic: הֵיאַךְ אֲנִי קוֹרֵא בֵּיהּ ״עַיִן תַּחַת עַיִן״?
phrases.english: how can I call this 'an eye for an eye'?

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַרְתָּ, הֲרֵי שֶׁהָיְתָה עֵינוֹ שֶׁל זֶה גְּדוֹלָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the proof for the position stated in step 30
steps.raayaSupportSource: The logic that eyes of different sizes cannot be an equal exchange

steps.title: One equal law means it must always be money
steps.stepSummary: Someone might say: use money only when the eyes are different sizes. But the Torah demands 'משפט אחד', one equal law for all, so it must always be money.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you would say: in every case like this, where the eyes are not equal, he takes money from him (but when the eyes are equal, we take a real eye). The Torah said: 'You shall have one law', meaning a law that is the same for all of you!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא blocks a way out of רבי דוסתאי's proof. You cannot split the law into money sometimes and a real eye other times.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 31 showed that taking a real eye does not work when the eyes are different sizes. Someone could answer that money is only for those uneven cases. The פסוק 'משפט אחד יהיה לכם' says the law must be the same for everyone, so the only rule that fits every case is money.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you would say. This brings up a possible answer so it can be knocked down.
One law, the same rule for all
That is equal or the same

steps.whatToRemember: רבי דוסתאי's full proof: a real eye cannot be fair in every case, and the Torah wants one equal law. So 'עין תחת עין' means money.

phrases.english: And if you would say:

phrases.aramaic: כָּל כִּי הַאי – שָׁקֵיל מִינֵּיהּ מָמוֹנָא;
phrases.english: in every case like this, he takes money from him;
phrases.notes: 'Like this' means when the two eyes are different sizes. The idea is that equal eyes would still mean taking a real eye.

phrases.english: the Torah said:
"You shall have one law"
phrases.notes: ויקרא 24:22

phrases.english: a law that is equal for all of you!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכִי תֵּימָא: כָּל כִּי הַאי – שָׁקֵיל מִינֵּיהּ מָמוֹנָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the proof from step 31 by closing off a possible way out.
steps.raayaObject: That 'עין תחת עין' always means money
steps.raayaSupportSource: The פסוק 'משפט אחד יהיה לכם' (ויקרא 24:22), which requires one equal law for everyone

steps.title: Maybe the Torah means taking away his sight
steps.stepSummary: The חכמים ask what the problem is. Maybe the Torah means: he took away sight, so we take away his sight, and eye size does not matter.
steps.simpleTranslation: They say: What is the difficulty? Perhaps he took away sight from him, and the Merciful One said we should take away sight from him!
steps.whatsHappening: The חכמים push back against רבי דוסתאי's proof. They say the uneven-eyes problem is not a real problem.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי דוסתאי's proof depended on the size of the eye. The חכמים say the Torah may be measuring sight, not size. Blinding a big eye and blinding a small eye both take away the same thing, sight, so the law would still be equal for everyone.

keyTerms.meaning: They say. This brings in a response, often from the חכמים of the בית מדרש.
What is the difficulty? Meaning there is no real problem here.
The Merciful One, a name for ה׳ as the One who gave the Torah

steps.confusionAlert: The חכמים here are not saying the הלכה is to take a real eye. They are only showing that this one proof does not work, because there is another way to read the פסוק.

phrases.english: They say: What is the difficulty?
Perhaps he took away sight from him,
so the Merciful One said we should take away sight from him!
phrases.notes: So the size of the eye does not matter. Sight is sight, and the law stays equal.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמְרִי: מַאי קוּשְׁיָא? דִּלְמָא נְהוֹרָא שְׁקַיל מִינֵּיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof from steps 31 and 32.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Only רבי דוסתאי's uneven-eyes proof. It does not decide the final הלכה.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The proof assumes the Torah measures the size of the eye. The Torah may instead be measuring sight, which is the same in every eye.

steps.title: Setting up support for the sight reading
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא begins an argument: 'For if you do not say so…'. It is about to show that the uneven-eyes reasoning would lead to something impossible.
steps.simpleTranslation: For if you do not say so,
steps.whatsHappening: This line is a setup. The גמרא is getting ready to support the חכמים' pushback, and the full argument comes in the next lines.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'דאי לא תימא הכי' means: if you do not accept that the Torah means taking away sight, a problem will follow. The גמרא is about to show that rejecting the sight reading leads to an impossible result. That would make the חכמים' pushback stronger.

phrases.english: For if you do not say so,
phrases.notes: 'So' means the idea that the Torah takes away sight, not a same-sized eye. The rest of the argument comes next.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a supporting argument for the pushback in step 33.
steps.raayaObject: That the Torah may mean taking away sight, no matter the size of the eye
steps.raayaSupportSource: An argument that rejecting this reading leads to an impossible result. It continues after this line.
